paras: The lynching of Jack Hopkins took place in Monticello, Jasper County, Georgia, in the last days of July 1885, when masked men shot Hopkins, a Black prisoner, to death through the openings of his jail cell. Hopkins had been arrested days earlier, accused of knifing his employer or a young white man. A coroner's jury attributed the death to unknown parties, and the killing ran in white papers across the country, some calling it a lynching and others the fate of a 'murderer'.

According to the Monticello wire, Hopkins quarreled with his employer, George Gilmore, described as a wealthy planter, and struck him on the head and attacked him with a knife while Gilmore tended his stock. The same account said Hopkins cut his way through half a dozen men who interrupted him and fled to the woods, and that a posse with dogs tracked him until Tuesday morning, July 28, when he was arrested at McDonough. The Savannah Morning News told the story differently, saying Hopkins had severely cut a young man in Jasper County about four weeks earlier.
Brought back bound hand and foot, he was placed in an iron cage in the Monticello jail, a 'Pauley's patent cell' with small openings for air and light.

In the wire's account, about twenty masked men rode up to the edge of town at 11 o'clock on Thursday night, July 30, and four of them, armed with double-barreled shotguns, went to the jail. As they approached, Hopkins begged for mercy; they put their muzzles to the ventilation openings, fired, reloaded, fired again and rode away. Townspeople roused by the volley saw four masked men running, while an earlier dispatch said the jailer learned of the killing only when he brought breakfast to the cell.

The Savannah correspondent placed the killing on Wednesday night and described one shooter, who called Hopkins by name and fired into his head by the light of a fire that others had kindled beside the jail.

Coroner Whitten summoned an inquest jury, which met on Tuesday, August 4, and examined twenty or thirty witnesses. Its verdict found that Hopkins died by a shot from a double-barreled shotgun 'in the hands of some unknown parties' and asked the Governor and County Commissioners to offer a reward. No warrant was issued, and the same report said Hopkins's wife intended to swear out a warrant against Gilmore for the killing and was rumored to plan a suit against the county. No report of arrests, a reward or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News headlined its report 'Monticello Vigilants Shoot a Black Desperado Through the Bars', calling the killing 'one of the most cold-blooded and diabolical murders ever committed in the State' while adding that 'the negro was a bad character'. In Georgia the Marietta Journal gave the case one line among state briefs, and the Yorkville Enquirer in South Carolina set it under 'Lynchings in Georgia' beside the Bainbridge lynching of a white man.

Elsewhere the long Monticello wire ran from August 1 in papers from New York and Ohio to Texas and Kansas, describing Hopkins as 'more like a wild animal than a man'. Headlines split: the New-York Tribune printed 'Lynched for a Light Offence' and the Waco Daily Examiner 'A Georgia Horror!', while the Fort Worth Daily Gazette wrote 'A Black Murderer Lynched By Masked Men' and the Dallas Daily Herald 'A Would-be Murderer ... Visited by Moonlight'. Condensed briefs in the following week said Hopkins had been held for the 'murder' of Gilmore, and a Sacramento item called the killers 'masked citizens'. No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.

Papers named the victim Jack, John or George Hopkins; the coroner's verdict printed in Savannah used 'Jack', while 'George' appears only in the first dispatch. Briefs that said Gilmore was murdered conflict with the fuller wire, which said he was struck and knifed, and with the later report that Hopkins's wife sought a warrant against him.

reader.title: Lynching of Jack Hopkins
bases: A band of about twenty masked men came to the Monticello jail at night and shot a jailed Black prisoner to death in his cell (A5, A8, A4).

Hopkins was shot dead in jail by masked 'unknown parties' numbering about twenty, four of whom fired according to the wire (A5, A8, A17); he was held on the accusation of knifing his employer or a young white man, and the killing was called a murder by 'Vigilants' in Georgia and a 'Lynching' in the Indianapolis headline (A4, A8).

The Savannah Morning News's Georgia correspondent, the Marietta Journal and the Monticello wire report the same killing in the same jail cell (A4, A16, A5), and the coroner's jury verdict confirms the death by shotgun (A17); they differ on details of the date, the name and the shooting.

accounts.label: Monticello wire (Aug. 1)
accounts.gist: About twenty masked men rode to the edge of town at 11 p.m. Thursday; four went to the jail, fired through the ventilation openings as Hopkins begged for mercy, reloaded, fired again and rode off.

accounts.label: Earlier Monticello dispatch (July 31)
accounts.gist: A masked gang rode in between 12 and 1 Friday morning and fired 'hundreds of buckshot' through the cell openings into George Hopkins; the jailer found him dead at breakfast.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News correspondent (Indian Springs)
accounts.gist: On Wednesday night unknown parties lit a fire on one side of the jail while one man, on the other side, woke Hopkins by name and fired a heavily loaded gun into his head.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death by a shot from a double-barreled shotgun by unknown parties; no warrant; a reward recommended.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Killed in His Cell. Monticello Vigilants Shoot a Black Desperado Through the Bars', called it among the most 'cold-blooded and diabolical murders' in the state, yet added that Hopkins 'was a bad character'.
Most papers ran the Monticello wire, which called Hopkins's alleged attack 'fiendish work' and described him as 'more like a wild animal than a man'.
The New-York Tribune headlined the dispatch 'Lynched for a Light Offence', and the Waco Daily Examiner called it 'A Georgia Horror!'.

Other headlines cast Hopkins as the offender: 'A Black Murderer Lynched By Masked Men' (Fort Worth), 'A Would-be Murderer ... Visited by Moonlight' (Dallas), 'Lynching of a Murderer in Georgia' (Indianapolis); a Sacramento brief called the killers 'masked citizens'.
The Yorkville Enquirer printed the dispatch under 'Lynchings in Georgia' after the Bainbridge lynching of a white man, and the Marietta Journal gave it one line among Georgia briefs.

conflicts.note: One man in every account; the coroner's verdict quoted in the Georgia press uses 'Jack Hopkins' and the same item calls him John, so Jack/John is best supported. 'George' appears only in the early dispatch, which may have confused him with his employer George Gilmore.
